title: Generic Pair
story: You're building a game and need to store pairs of values: a player name with their score (Str, Int), coordinates (Float64, Float64), and an item name with whether it's equipped (Str, Bool). Three different pairs, same structure. You need a reusable Pair type.
why: Generic types like `Pair[T,U]` let you create reusable data structures — define the shape once, use it with any combination of types.
analogy: A generic Pair is like a two-pocket folder. One pocket is labeled 'first' and the other 'second.' You decide what goes in each pocket: money and receipts (Int, Str), photos and dates (Str, Str), or tickets and stubs (Str, Bool). The folder structure is always the same — two pockets — but the contents can be anything.
try_it: Create a Pair of Str and Bool for a feature toggle: name and enabled status. Add a `describe` method on Pair[Str,Bool] that returns a descriptive string. Create a `Triple[T,U,V]` type with three fields. Write a function that takes a Vec of Pairs and returns a Pair of Vecs (separating firsts from seconds).
tips: Use different letters for different type parameters: `Pair[T,U]` means two possibly-different types, `Pair[T,T]` means both must be the same
Type parameters on types go in brackets after the type NAME: `type Pair[T,U] = { ... }`
When creating a generic type instance, specify the concrete types: `Pair[Str,Int]{ first: ..., second: ... }`
common_mistakes: Forgetting to specify type arguments when creating: `Pair{ first: "a", second: 1 }` doesn't tell XIOM what T and U are
Using `T` for both fields when they should be different types — `Pair[T]` has one type; `Pair[T,U]` has two
Accessing `.third` on a Pair — it only has `.first` and `.second`
